name: The Hamilton household
head: hamilton_richard_j

arrival.note: Andreas's list of the town's lawyers gives the year and no month: 'Richard J. Hamilton, 1831'.

party_size_on_arrival.note: Not attested. Hamilton had a family at Chicago - his daughter Mrs Ellen Hamilton Keenon has her own biographical entry in Andreas - but no source reached counts the party that travelled with him in 1831.

origin.note: Not attested in anything this project holds.

reason_for_coming.value: County office and a law practice in a new county seat
reason_for_coming.note: Cook County was organised in 1831 and Hamilton is its clerk from that year, which is the ordinary reading of a lawyer arriving in the year the county is created. INFERRED: no source states his motive.

lives_at.note: DOCUMENTED FOR 1832 AND NOT FOR THE SCENE DATE, which is why this is graded derived rather than documented. Andreas, on the founding of the first school: 'In the fall of 1832, Colonel Hamilton and Colonel Owen employed John Watkins to teach a small school in the North Division, near the old Indian agency-house in which Colonel Hamilton then resided.' That is a plain statement that he lived in the building this dataset records as cobweb_castle, and it is nearly three years before 1 July 1835. Nothing reached follows him out of it or keeps him in it. The link is made because it is the only attested residence for any named person in that building and because an unlinked household teaches a reader nothing; the grade is the warning.

works_at.note: The county's business was done wherever the clerk kept his papers, and the brick court-house on the square was not finished until the autumn of 1835 - after the scene date. This dataset holds cook_county_courthouse_1835 as a building under way, not as an office in use on 1 July, so no work link is made.

present_on_scene_date.note: In office continuously through the period and named in Chicago business across 1833-36; no absence is recorded.

persons.name: Richard Jones Hamilton

occupation.note: Clerk of the Cook County Commissioners' Court and, in 1833, commissioner for the sale of the school section; Andreas also lists him among the town's six lawyers at the close of 1833 (scan p. 281). The office is the better-attested of the two and is what this record carries; the practice is in the note.

persons.note: ONE OF THE SIX MEN ANDREAS COUNTS AS CHICAGO'S LAWYERS AT THE END OF 1833, and one of the twelve who voted for incorporation on 5 August 1833. Andreas, scan p. 281: 'It comprised six lawyers - Russel E. Heacock, who had come in 1827; Richard J. Hamilton, 1831; and Giles Spring, John Dean Caton, Edward W. Casey and Alexander N. Fullerton, who had put out their signs in 1833.' He administered the oath of office to the first board of trustees as a notary public and acted as its clerk pro tem, and he ran the auction of the school section in October 1833 with John Bates as auctioneer. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Hamilton, R. J.” (poll_1833_013, line 34); Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Hamilton, Richard J.” (tax_1833_042, line 94); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Hamilton, Richard J.” (poll_1834_049, line 218). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Hamilton' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 7 times, as “HAMILTON RICHARD J”, “HAMILTON R J”, 1833-10-22 to 1836-06-29: 5 lots in the platted town — lot 1 of block 8 in the town the register codes CHIV (L1BL8CHIV, as printed); lot 2 of block 8 in the town the register codes CHIV (L2BL8CHIV, as printed); lot 4 of block 2 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L4BL2CHIOT, as printed); the N2 of lot 7 of block 2 in the town the register codes CHIV (N2L7BL2CHIV, as printed); the S2 of lot 7 of block 3 in the town the register codes CHI (S2L7BL3CHI, as printed) and 2 parcels of the school section — lot 5 of block 2 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 6 of block 25 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $17236.00 (ls0225, ls0226, ls1203, ls1204, ls1205, ls1206, ls1207). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $17160.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: HAMILTON RICHARD J matches Richard Jones Hamilton: the forename names Richard Jones Hamilton of the 3 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

refusals.reason: This card rests on 3 thing(s) the consolidation did not read — andreas_1884_v1, census_1840_chicago_familysearch_images, chicago_democrat_1833_1835. G2b fired on the seven domains the ladder reads and says nothing about the evidence outside them, so the grade stands. The same reasoning the ladder's own G5 gives for abstaining (T-0515).

resident_research.summary: The 1833 poll ('Hamilton, R. J.'), the 1833 tax list and the 1834 poll (both 'Hamilton, Richard J.') all match, one bearer of the surname considered. The Cook County history read in pass 2 gives the offices — clerk and recorder from the county's organisation in 1831, later probate judge, treasurer and school commissioner — and pass 2 never wrote it into a ledger.

roles.note: THE BOUND IS THE SOURCE'S, NOT THE MAN'S. This role is carried by the card's 1835 occupation block and is dated by what the cited source or sources are ABOUT, which is why `precision` can be no better than the span they cover. The span reaches 1835, so this role stands in the scene-date view. The printing the trade was read off is not on the card and is fetched by T-1254.

research_note: THE COUNTY'S CLERK, AND THE ONE NAMED PERSON THIS PROJECT CAN PUT INSIDE COBWEB CASTLE. The residence link is the point of the record and it is also its weakness: the sentence that supplies it is about a schoolmaster's employment in 1832, and it is doing double duty here as evidence about a building and about a household. Graded derived on both counts. A SECOND THING THIS RECORD DOES NOT CLAIM: Hamilton appears constantly in the 1833-35 record as commissioner, notary, clerk pro tem and attorney, and it would be easy to write him a household of five and an origin. Nothing supports either.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. WHAT THIS PASS RULED ONTO THIS HOUSEHOLD, named so the ruling can be found again: each volume below is followed by the printed entries it set against this person and the status the crosswalk ruled them at — a single entry carries what its own `could_carry` declares, and an ambiguous or contested match carries nothing and is shown so that the silence is legible. hamilton_richard_j, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 — f1839_e0626 (a single entry); hamilton_richard_j, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 — f1843_e1188 (a single entry); hamilton_richard_j, Norris's Chicago directory of 1844 — n1844_e0782 (a single entry).

address_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints this address against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Hamilton, Rich’d J., clerk circuit court, Clark st cor. Randolph'. It is evidence about 1839, written here as 1839's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.

back_projection.note: A LATER ADDRESS, READ BACKWARDS 4 YEARS. The door is not an 1835 reading: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 printed it in 1839, and this pass carries it back to the scene date because the 1835 record attests a trade for this person and nothing in the corpus places it better. What is claimed is the corner where the two streets cross and nothing narrower — no lot, no roof, no door count — and the grade is `reconstructed`, which is this dataset's word for a figure the reconstruction supplies rather than a source. Clark Street and Randolph Street both stand in 1835 under those names, and the directory sets the door AT their corner, which is the point where the two committed centrelines cross. The rule this stands on is docs/ADDRESS-BACK-PROJECTION.md and the liberty is L218; a reader who thinks 4 years is too far to carry a shop should read the grade as the disagreement being invited.
